## C.2. The mathematical complexity

As quickly mentioned earlier, a few algorithms are directly interpretable by their mathematical nature. There are 3 of them: the linear regression, the logistic regression and the simple decision tree. By getting the regression coefficients we have direct access to the feature importance foe the model (global interpretability) and we can apply those coefficients to each prediction to get the local interpretability. The decision tree also gives us directly the underlying rules of the model.

On the other hand, many algorithms are not directly interpretable, that is the case of most models used : Ensemble models (Random Forest, XGBoost ... ), SVM, Artificial Neural Networks ... In these cases, we have to use additional toolboxes like Lime or Shap (that we will describe later) to access the model and prediction interpretability.

It is important to note that already existing regulations (for finance and insurance for example) and the one to come from the UE impose the use of directly interpretable models for critical systems i.e. the ones with a potential effect on users' interests.

## C.3. Direct interpretability

## C.3.a. Regressions

You get the direct interpretability for regressions (either for classifications or regressions) by looking at the coefficients. You get the coefficient in Sklearn with 'model.coef_'. You can put them in a DataFrame with the variable names for simpler visualization : pd. DataFrame ( {"Feature": X_train . columns . tolist () , "Coefficients" : model. coef [0]}

Don't forget to standardize your data first!

You can normalize your data by centering or scaling

First, normalizing allows interpretation of variable coefficients associated with different magnitudes, e.g. when one regressor is measured on a very small order, while another on a very large order. Standardization allows the units of regression coefficients to be expressed in the same units. Luckily, centering or scaling does not have an impact on p-values, therefore regression model statistics can be interpreted the same way as if centering or scaling did not take place.

## 4. Explainability pillar

### Core concept Explain a model's decision/prediction through a user/business interface

What are the risks?

· For your business customers > non-adoption of a solution, mistrust

· For your end customers > dissatisfaction, lack of information

· For your organization > impact on productivity and business

Where do you start?

V Build UX with and according to the business needs and business language (=medical terms for doctors, financial terms for banks, etc.)

V Implement almost systematic requests for feedback

(= business user satisfaction survey)

What's the competitive advantage?

· For your customers > trust

· For your organization > robustness, maintenance, compliance (with GDPR and the Al Act, for instance, which also apply to organizations, in particular the GAFAM, operating on European soil)

## INTERPRETABILITY, EXPLAINABILITY: WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE?

The interpretability pillar consists in configuring an algorithmic model to allow access to the factors that influence predictions/decisions throughout the Al lifecycle. This work is carried out by a data scientist.

The explainability pillar consists in explaining the results (derived from interpretability) to the users of an Al solution (so that they can understand them and adopt the solution).

## KEEP HUMANS IN THE LOOP

It refers to the practice of preserving human involvement and oversight in the decision-making processes of artificial intelligence systems. This involvement ensures accountability and helps prevent potential biases or errors in Al-driven decisions. Moreover, by preserving the fundamental human need for control and agency in decision- making processes, it fosters adoption of the solution.

## CUSTOMER STORIES: CRAFTING EXPLAINABLE SOLUTIONS FOR ENHANCED ADOPTION THROUGH USER-CENTRIC APPROACHES

· Challenge: We build all our solutions with explainability by design. For users, to understand where the recommendations of the algorithms are coming from is key for trust and adoption. For example, we have two customers from very different industries (food and publishing) both wanting a solution displaying the performance of their point of sales on interactive maps.

. Approach: Different types of users, from different businesses, need different types of information. User experience interviews are essential to understand their specific needs, and frequent user tests during the development allow the interface to be tweaked to be as relevant as possible.

. Outcome: The interfaces produced for both clients were very different, addressing the specific needs of each, increasing user satisfaction and adoption rates. This method establishes a foundation of trust through customized interfaces, that is adapted to diverse user needs.

A recent study by Nezhurina et al. revealed significant deficiencies in the reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), which were trained at the largest available scales and claimed to possess strong functional abilities.275 When presented with a simple, concise common- sense problem, easily solvable by humans, these models frequently failed to provide correct solutions. Standard interventions, such as enhanced prompting or multistep re-evaluation, were ineffective in correcting these errors. ## C.5. Performance/Interpretability Trade-off

Often, more complex models give better performance. Especially for complex datasets, XGBoost for example will perform better than a simple decision tree. But that added complexity leads to the loss of the interpretability. We talk about the Performance / Interpretability Trade-off.

Source: figure from Arrieta et al. 2019 that you can find here: Re (PDF) Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): Concepts, Taxonomies, Opportunities and Challenges toward Responsible AI

We highly recommend reading this paper for more information on the subject.

There is no general guideline to follow to resolve this trade-off, it is a case-by-case consideration to make. Depending on the risk/criticality for the users of the model you are building and the regulation in place, you might not have a choice to go for a directly interpretable algorithm. In the other cases, it is always better to start simple and to increase the complexity until reaching a satisfying level of performance.

<!-- PageBreak -->

# D. Toolboxes for indirect interpretability

There are many tools to 'open the black box' and get information about the model, but keep in mind that there are all indirect variable estimations and are just indications and certainly not exact information.

Most of these techniques are universal (model agnostic) and can be applied to all algorithms/models. However, certain tools are better suited for certain types of data and certain type of models. We will mainly focus on two toolboxes: Lime and SHAP as there are the ones most widely used.

## D.1. Structured data

For structured data, and for models that are not directly interpretable, we suggest the use of these two toolboxes, LIME and Shap.

## D.1.a. LIME

The acronym LIME stands for Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations. It provides local interpretability for your classifications and can be applied to any model. It is based on this paper : https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.04938.pdf and you can also watch this video for a high-level explanation : KDD2016 paper 573

LIME uses a local surrogate model trained on perturbations of the data point we are investigating for explanations.

Source : https://github.com/marcotcr/lime

Even though we can use any interpretable model as the local surrogate, the paper uses a Lasso regression to induce sparsity in explanations.

The advantages of the technique are:

· Both the methodology and the explanations are very intuitive to explain to a human being.

· It is Model-agnostic.

. It works for structured as well as unstructured data (more on that later).

· Available in R and Python (original implementation by the authors of the paper).

<!-- PageBreak -->

Here is how the algorithm works:

· In order to find an explanation for a single data point and a given classifier, it samples the locality around the selected single data point uniformly and at random and generate a dataset of perturbed data points with its corresponding prediction from the model we want to explain.

· Then it uses the specified feature selection methodology to select the number of features that is required for the explanation.

· It calculates the sample weights using a kernel function and a distance function (this captures how close or how far are the sampled points from the original point).

· It then fits an interpretable model (the Lasso regression) on the perturbed dataset using the sample weights to weigh the objective function.

· Finally, it provides local explanations using the newly trained interpretable model.

It provides nice visualizations of the local interpretability like this example taken from this tutorial : Tutorial - continuous and categorical features from LIME's authors:

This is analyzing the Iris dataset, with a Random Forest, after training an 'explainer' like that:

explainer = lime. lime_tabular. LimeTabularExplainer (train, feature_names=iris. feature_names,

class_names=iris. target_names, discretize_continuous=True)

exp = explainer. explain_instance (test [i], rf.predict_proba, num_features=2, top_labels=1)

This figure tells you that, for this instance,(1) the Random Forest model predicted the label 'setosa' with a probability of 1 (left part of the image), (2) it did no because the petal width was smaller or equal to 0.30cm and its length less than 1.6cm (central part of the image) and (3) it gives you the feature values highlighting the important features.

For more details, you can look at:

. The tutorial: Tutorial - continuous and categorical features

· This article: https://towardsdatascience.com/lime-how-to-interpret-machine- learning-models-with-python-94b0e7e4432e

<!-- PageFooter: D.1.b. SHAP -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

### D.2.c. Attention Interpretability

Quite often nowadays, deep neural networks are used for NLP tasks. This allows for specific interpretability if you use attention networks. Indeed, attention layer in a neural network can give you insight into the model's prediction by obtaining the weights in a specific layer. It works for example with BERT and other Transformers.

The interpretability power of these methods is under discussion, we won't go into the details here, but you should know it is a possibility.

Here are some more or less scientific papers about this:

· Deconstructing BERT, Part 2: Visualizing the Inner Workings of Attention

· https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.04840.pdf

## D.3. Images

As for text, images also have specific functions from LIME and SHAP, and also, attention layers of some Deep Learning Networks can be used.

## D.3.a. LIME

As for tabular data, LIME generates perturbations in order to see the impact on the model decision and see what part of the image is crucial for the prediction. Here is an illustration of the process:

<!-- PageBreak -->

The way to implement LIME for image is similar to everything we have seen before. Here we use an example for their official tutorial (Lime Images ), which is based on inception v3. We will look at the interpretability of this image:

The multilabel predictions for the top 5 classes are: 286 Egyptian cat 0.000892741

Let's look at how to visualize the interpretation. First initiate the Explainer and get the explanation:

Now let see the explanation for the top class (Bernese mountain dog)

temp, mask = explanation. get_image_and_mask(240, positive_only=True, num_features=5, hide_rest=True) plt.imshow(mark_boundaries(temp / 2 + 0.5, mask))

We can also look at the part of the image in favor (green) and in disfavor (red) of the top class:

temp, mask = explanation.get_image_and_mask (240, positive_only=False, num_features=10, hide_rest=False) plt.imshow (mark_boundaries (temp / 2 + 0.5, mask) )

## A. For whom?

<!-- PageBreak -->

### A.1. The regulator

As mentioned in the section about legal risks in Introduction, the new European law on AI will describe different levels of criticality for AI models. Depending on the level, complete or partial interpretability will be asked by law and in addition to documentation, some audits might occur. Therefore, interpretability will become mandatory for many AI models.

### A.2. The developer or Data Scientist

The data scientist needs to access, as best as possible, the parameters of a model to understand it, to fix possible mistakes, to improve its performance and to stay in control.

#### A.3. The main user

The user needs information in order to best use the product or solution as well as to trust its recommendation. Adoption is driven by trust and very linked to the information that will be provided. We will get into more details about that in the Explicability section of these Guidelines.

#### A.4. The final user

The final user is the person who is the subject of the prediction or decision. That can be the same person as the main user or a different one. For example, we can have a skin diagnostic solution for doctors (main users) that concerns their patients (final users). This group of people may ask for information about the decision/prediction of the algorithm and in many case, they have the legal right to know what were the factor that lead to the decision/prediction.

# B. Of what?

We can be interested to have interpretability of the whole system or just of different parts of the system. We can look to understand a single prediction, all predictions, a part of the model, the whole model, the path that the data takes along the processing pipeline ...

## B.1. Global and Local

<!-- PageBreak -->

There are two main information that we want to access when we talk about Interpretability. We want to access what factors influenced each prediction and with what extend, that is called the Local Interpretability, and we also want to know what the factors of importance for the model are, that is the Global Interpretability.

In the case of simple algorithms like the regressions, the global interpretability is directly given by the coefficients of the model after training (remember to scale or normalize your data first, overwise you will not be able to interpret the results). With sklearn, just use 'model.coef_'. You can put them in a DataFrame with the variable names for simpler visualization :

pd. DataFrame ( {"Feature" : X_train . columns . tolist () , "Coefficients" : model . coef [0]})

In the case of more complex models, we will need to use additional tools to have access to an approximation of this information, like Lime or Shap or the Feature Importance function of sklearn. N.B. LIME and SHAP are local interpretability methods but they can still be used for the global interpretability.

You can refer to the sklearn MOOC part on feature importance here for more

information: Feature importance - Scikit-learn course

For the interpretability of the predictions (local), we see the same distinction between simple and more complex algorithms. With the simple models, we can directly apply the coefficients or the rules (for simple decision tree) to the data specific for each individual prediction. For more complex algorithms, we will again use additional tools (Lime, Shap ... ).

We will come back to the tools in more details in a dedicated section.

# C. Why not interpretable?

## C.1. The data complexity

There are different ways in which the data itself can make the system hard to interpret.

Some variables may contain information that is difficult to comprehend, for example medical or scientific information or expert technical measurements.

Moreover, during the Feature Engineering of the model construction, we may apply manipulations to the data that may lead to a loss of meaning. For example taking the log of a measure, using a dimension reduction method (i.e. PCA), combining variables ...

<!-- PageBreak -->

Finally, the storage of the data can add to the complexity if we lose the lineage and the contextual information that goes with it.

shap_values = explainer (X)

The first interesting plot is the Waterfall: # visualize the first prediction's explanation shap.plots.waterfall (shap_values [0] )

You can see the influence of each feature, with their direction and magnitude.

Another, more condensed way to illustrate the same thing is the 'force plot': # visualize the first prediction's explanation with a force plot shap.plots. force (shap_values [0])

This is probably the most used visualization of the library.

To understand how a single feature effects the output of the model, we can plot the SHAP value of that feature vs. the value of the feature for all the examples in a dataset. It is a similar approach to Partial Dependency Plot (PDP). In the example here, we are looking at the effect of the number of rooms ('RM') # create a dependence scatter plot to show the effect of a single feature across

the whole dataset shap. plots . scatter (shap_values [ :, "RM"], color=shap_values)

Since SHAP values represent a feature's responsibility for a change in the model output, this plot represents the change in predicted house price as RM (the average number of rooms per house in an area) changes. You can try to understand the variability observed for a single value of RM with its interaction effects with other features. To help reveal these interactions we can color by another feature. If we pass the whole explanation tensor to the color argument the scatter plot will pick the best feature to color by. In this case it picks RAD (index of accessibility to radial highways) since that highlights that the average number of rooms per house has less impact on home price for areas with a high RAD value.

SHAP can also give you the global interpretability of your model.

<!-- PageBreak -->

To do so, we can plot the SHAP values of every feature for every sample. This can be done with the Beeswarm plot. It sorts features by the sum of SHAP value magnitudes over all samples, and uses SHAP values to show the distribution of the impacts each feature has on the model output. The color represents the feature value (red high, blue low). This reveals for example that a high LSTAT (% lower status of the population) lowers the predicted home price. # summarize the effects of all the features shap.plots.beeswarm (shap_values)

Finally, we can also just take the mean absolute value of the SHAP values for each feature to get a standard 'feature importance' bar plot: shap.plots. bar (shap_values)

It is important to note that SHAP designed specific solution for Tree based models (all the way to XGBoost), with their shap.TreeExplainer(model).

We won't go into the details here, but you can find the documentation here : Tabular examples - SHAP latest documentation, and their Nature paper on the subject here: https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-019-0138-9

Overall, SHAP is a very good library, offering many ways to visualize your interpretability compared to LIME, so why consider LIME? As we already mentioned, the advantage of LIME over SHAP is SPEED. The two methods emerge very differently. LIME perturbs data around an individual prediction to build a model, while SHAP has to compute all permutations globally to get local accuracy.

## D.1.c. Other methods

They are many other interpretability methods, we will not get into the details, we will refer you to this online book by Christoph Molnar: Interpretable Machine Learning

We will still list them here to be exhaustive.

### Global Model-Agnostic Methods:

· The partial dependence plot is a feature effect method.

· Accumulated local effect plots is another feature effect method that works when features are dependent.

<!-- PageBreak -->

· Feature interaction (H-statistic) quantifies to what extent the prediction is the result of joint effects of the features.

· Functional decomposition is a central idea of interpretability and a technique that decomposes the complex prediction function into smaller parts.

· Permutation feature importance measures the importance of a feature as an increase in loss when the feature is permuted.

· Global surrogate models replaces the original model with a directly interpretable model for interpretation.

· Prototypes and criticisms are representative data point of a distribution and can be used to enhance interpretability.

Local Model-Agnostic Methods:

· Individual conditional expectation curves are the building blocks for partial dependence plots and describe how changing a feature changes the prediction.

· Scoped rules (anchors) are rules that describe which feature values anchor a prediction, in the sense that they lock the prediction in place.

· Counterfactual explanations explain a prediction by examining which features would need to be changed to achieve a desired prediction.

· Shapley values are an attribution method that fairly assigns the prediction to individual features.

You initiate the explainer, after having trained a model for sentient analysis for example:

exp = explainer. explain_instance(text, model. predict_proba, num_features=6) And you get that illustration:

It gives you the usual LIME plot with the prediction probabilities of the model for this prediction (on the left) and what were the features (here words) important for the prediction.

This important addition is the highlighted text at the bottom of the figure, that shows you the words, in the sentence, that were important, color coded as a function of the possible labels (here blue for positive, orange for negative sentiment).

As for tabular data, LIME is easy to use and relatively fast.

## D.2.b. SHAP

The process with SHAP is very similar, there are just more visualization options. You

can access the documentation here : Text examples - SHAP latest documentation , from which we took the following examples.

You start with the explainer on your pretrained model: explainer = shap. Explainer (pred)

You compute the shap values for a specific instance: shap_values = explainer (data [ ' text ' ] [ : 0] )

And you visualize the result: shap. plots. text (shap_values)

# 3- Interpretability

Machine Learning changed the way computer programs are done. Developers used to formalize a problem and code the rules that would transform input data into output data. Now, it is the model that determines the rules that link the input and output data through iterations and error minimization. It is this ability that gives all its power to Machine Learning and allows us to solve problems that exceed human formalization capabilities. But it is also coupled with a constraint: the rules applied by the model after training to make its predictions and decision may evade human control. For certain types of models, these rules sometimes remain unknown, even if interpretability techniques have made great progress in recent years. This is the famous "black box effect". However, when we decide to use Al to make decisions or make predictions that will have an impact on the lives of citizens, it is crucial, and soon to be regulatory, to keep control of the models and guarantee their explicability.

The interpretability of AI models is therefore becoming a major challenge, both for those who design them and for those who use them. It is a question of knowing which factors influence each decision and prediction (local interpretability) but also which rules govern the model in general (global interpretability).

Interpretability can be defined as having access to the features or variables that are driving the decisions or predictions of a model.

An Interpretable system becomes:

· Explicable: we can provide information and explanation (see the Explicability section)

· Transparent: it has a functioning intelligible to a human

· Provable: it can provide proof of the accuracy of the result

Whatever your use-case, it is critical to use interpretability methods.

If your system is critical, you should use directly interpretable models (regressions or simple decision trees), you can refer to Section 3.C.Direct Interpretability for more information.

If you are not required Direct Interpretability, are decided to use more complex models, you can use toolboxes to access indirect interpretability. You can refer to Section 3.D for more information, depending on the type of data (tabular, text or images).

#### 3.1.3.A. The black box problem

Opacity surrounding the technical, internal decision- making processes of generative Al models is popularly known as the "black box problem."277 Generative Al models, most ubiquitously built on deep neural networks with hundreds of billions of internal connections,278 have become so complex that their internal decision-making processes are no longer traceable or interpretable to even the most advanced expert observers. This means that, while the inputs and outputs of a system can be observed, developers cannot explain in detail why specific inputs correspond to specific outputs.279

Increasing interpretability (i.e., the comprehension of how an Al model generates a specific output) is crucial. For developers and model trainers, understanding how models make decisions allows them to identify and correct biases, errors, and unintended behaviors, leading to more robust and efficient systems. This ability to anticipate and mitigate errors ensures that Al outputs are accurate and ethically sound. For lay people who use Al models, interpretability empowers them to make informed decisions and detect when the Al might be malfunctioning or producing biased outputs, enabling timely corrective actions. This reduces the risk of relying on faulty Al recommendations and fosters confidence in using these technologies. For individuals impacted by Al decisions, such as in healthcare, education, and finance, interpretability ensures that they can understand and challenge incorrect outcomes. Overall, increasing

interpretability helps prevent and mitigate unforeseen negative consequences, making Al systems more transparent, reliable, and aligned with societal values.

In the future, Al models may become less opaque. The field of explainable AI (XAI) seeks to develop new techniques and methods to improve the ability of users to comprehend the inner workings of Al models. 280 For instance, Anthropic has achieved a breakthrough to enhance the interpretability of language models.281 Instead of focusing on individual neurons, researchers at Anthropic analyze groups of neurons as features, revealing clearer patterns. Recently, Anthropic's researchers managed to extract millions of features from one of their Al models, creating a rough conceptual map of the model's internal states. 282 This approach may improve transparency and control over Al behavior.

#### 3.1.3.B. Industry opacity

Opacity is not solely due to the technological complexity that limits developers' and users' understanding of how generative models function on a technical level. It is further exacerbated by the practices of organizations and companies that are advancing the field. Many are private companies that choose to withhold from the public many of the precise characteristics of their most advanced models. Al developers cite both near-term competition and security risks to justify withholding many vital details of their models from the general public. SHAP stands for SHapley Additive explanations. They define their approach as: 'is a game theoretic approach to explain the output of any machine learning model. It connects optimal credit allocation with local explanations using the classic Shapley values from game theory and their related extensions'. We are going to try to be a bit clearer but it is definitely less intuitive than LIME.

Game theory is a theoretical framework for social situations among competing players. It is the science of optimal decision-making of independent and competing actors in a strategic setting. A "Game" is any situation in which there are several decision-makers, and each of them wants to optimize their results. The optimizing decision will depend on the decisions of others. The game identifies the players' identities, preferences, and available strategies and how these strategies affect the outcome.

In essence, Game Theory is a way to mathematically model complex human behavior, to try to understand it, and predict it. You can read more about game theory and it's fit in the AI world in this article : Game (Theory) for AI? An Illustrated Guide for Everyone .

Applied to Machine Learning, we know that each value of an independent variable or a feature for a given sample is a part of a cooperative game where we assume that prediction is actually the payout. So, let's use an example to understand this in detail.

Assume the following scenario:

We have trained a machine learning model to predict apartment prices in Paris. For a certain apartment, our model predicts 250K euros and we need to explain this prediction. This apartment is 75m2, 2 bedrooms, on the 3rd floor. The average prediction for all apartments is 210K euros. How much has each feature value contributed to the prediction compared to the average prediction?

Now, if we talk in terms of Game Theory, the "game" here is the prediction task for a single instance of the dataset. The "players" are the feature values of the instance that collaborate to play the game (predict a value).

In our example, the feature values 'square_meters, nb_bedrooms and floor' worked together to achieve the prediction of 250K euros. Our goal is to explain the difference between the actual prediction (250K euros) and the average prediction (210K euros): a difference of 40K euros.

A possible explanation could be 'square_meters' contributed 20K euros, 'nb_bedrooms' contributed 10K euros, and 'floor' contributed 10K euros. The contributions add up to 40K - the prediction minus the average predicted house price.

<!-- PageBreak -->

The Shapley value for each variable (payout) is basically trying to find the correct weight such that the sum of all Shapley values is the difference between the predictions and average value of the model. In other words, Shapley values correspond to the contribution of each feature towards pushing the prediction away from the expected value.

Here is the intuitive explanation of the Shapley values, for more details please refer to :

· The Shap librairy documentation:

Welcome to the SHAP documentation - SHAP latest documentation

· The github page:

GitHub - shap/shap: A game theoretic approach to explain the output of any machine learning model.

· A good article explaining how it works:

Interpretable Machine Learning using SHAP-theory and applications

· And this article for a slightly different view:

Understanding SHAP for Interpretable Machine Learning

Computing shapley values takes more time than LIME, but the library comes with more useful types of visualizations that we will describe here. The examples used are coming from their github (GitHub - shap/shap: A game theoretic approach to explain the output of any machine learning model. )

There are different methods of shapley values approximation depending on the type of method we are trying to explain : KernelSHAP, DeepSHAP and TreeSHAP.

First of all, using SHAP is extremely easy, and it can be used on any model. Here is a snipet of code for XGBoost on the Boston Housing Dataset: import xgboost

import shap # train an XGBoost model

X, y = shap.datasets.boston ()

model = xgboost. XGBRegressor () . fit (X, y)

# explain the model's predictions using SHAP (same syntax works for LightGBM, CatBoost, scikit-learn, transformers, Spark, etc.) explainer = shap. Explainer (model)

## 09 APPENDICES

### APPENDIX 1: GLOSSARY

· Accountability: Accountability can be broken down into two subcomponents: answerability and auditability. Answerability refers to establishing a continuous chain of human responsibility across the whole AI project delivery workflow and demands that explanations and justifications of both the content of algorithmically supported decisions and the processes behind their production be offered by competent human authorities in plain, understandable, and coherent language. Auditability answers the question of how the designers and implementers of AI systems are to be held accountable. This aspect of accountability has to do with demonstrating both the responsibility of design and use practices and the justifiability of outcomes.

· Algorithm: An algorithm is a procedure or series of steps that provide instructions on how to take a series of inputs and produce an output. For instance, a recipe can be thought of as an algorithm that provides instructions for taking a series of inputs (i.e. the ingredients) and creating an output (e.g. a cake). In the case of machine learning, the algorithm is typically a series of instructions that instruct a software package to take a dataset (i.e. the input) and learn a model or discover some underlying pattern (i.e. the output).

# 4- Explicability

As described in introduction, AI is a system, with users to take into account and an interface to build. Once you have access to what factor influenced your prediction/decision, it comes the time to explain it to your users. That is what explicability is. Knowing your users, understanding not only their needs but their reluctances, choosing the right level of information, giving them control and ability to give feedbacks, all of these techniques will ensure more trust and adoption of your solution.

# A. UX studies

You need to know the appetite of users relative to AI to deliver the right level of explicability.

With explicability, we enter into UX Design and question the preference of users in terms of presentation of results. The level of explicability that accompanies the decision must correspond to the profile of the users. Depending on how AI will impact their work and life, but also on their maturity vis-à-vis this technology, not everyone will need the same granularity in the explanation.

To know the appetite of your users for AI, the best thing is to ask them the question through a short questionnaire. This will make it possible to detect the populations towards which it will be necessary to make a special effort to achieve genuine support.

Moreover, you won't give the same information to an expert or a novice. For example, for a medical diagnostic algorithm, you won't give the same information to doctors or patients. Doctors will need more technical information, patients more plain English ones. Workshops with your users and regular feedbacks are indispensable to fit your interface with their information requirements to trust your solution.

# B. Probabilities

By highlighting the relevant information, giving the user as much context as possible, it becomes possible to erase the feeling of no longer having any control over the decisions made by the machine.

The first information that will interest the user is to know how reliable the AI recommendation is. We too often set a default decision (i.e. threshold of 50% for a binary decision), and only give users the final decision: yes or no. results.content: ## · And mitigating AI risks is a true challenge in business adoption Hallucination, bias, confidentiality: these are the risks and limits that are holding companies back from using AI, through a healthy respect for both the regulatory framework, and a context where the acceptable margin of error in decision-making is low. So what do we mean by this? · Hallucination: generative Als are based on a multitude of documents. When the next word to predict matches the truth, all is well. But otherwise? They must choose one option, and can hallucinate untruths with great aplomb. Users therefore need to be trained to use these AIs properly, and to verify every single claim they make. . Bias: they are rarely intentional, but algorithmic biases are based on data reflecting human practice. The system can therefore discriminate against a specific group of people. A major obstacle for businesses is to identify potential biases (lack of qualified data), raise awareness among employees and have the resources to do so (a dedicated inclusive team, for instance, or a taxonomy programmed with contextual information), and then deal with the biases. . Privacy: The confidentiality rules of GenAl, and ChatGPT in particular, are still poorly understood. Bear in mind that any data and/or code sent to one of these platforms is likely to be used for subsequent training, which raises issues of confidentiality of corporate data (or that of its customers) and intellectual property. Overcoming these risks is not an option, it's a sine qua non condition for some businesses. However, the adoption of AI itself is facilitated when it is designed responsibly from the outset: ethical standards reinforce confidence in its use; responsible practices in critical sectors such as human resources guarantee a positive and equitable societal impact; operational excellence prevents abuse and ensures that the AI is beneficial and reliable... Adopting a responsible AI is thus becoming a crucial approach to minimizing risk. ## . Key Issue ### How do we turn this AI revolution into a competitive advantage? We need new "software" to tackle this profound change in the way we work, and even in the way we do business. New responsible governance must overcome all the risks generated by the use of AI and generative AI. By evolving into an "AI-ready" business, organizations put in place the conditions that will enable them to meet the key business challenges of the future, and perpetuate their business practices and even their business model. It's a moment of truth for organizations: yes, there is a turning point ahead; yet it does not have to be a problem: by implementing a "responsible-by-design" approach, organizations are better equipped to deal with the risks -not just compliance risks, but also business risks- created by the exploding use of Al (see pillars). Ekimetrics intends to accompany this revolution with a simple, easy-to-understand framework to support these organizations in their AI transformation and the use of these technologies. We have therefore developed 7 pillars of responsible AI, designed to create this competitive edge (see next chapter). ## · Empower business with AI and GenAI solutions through responsible governance Anticipate future regulations, limit the risk of damage to image and reputation, improve the efficiency, accuracy and durability of models, all while generating value: to meet all these challenges, Ekimetrics has developed 7 pillars of responsible governance, which can be considered true operational and business tools. THE 7 PILLARS OF RESPONSIBLE AI AND THEIR BUSINESS ADVANTAGES 1. Security Ensure the security of personal and sensitive data. GDPR compliance. Data Clean Rooms: value of personal data. 2. Transparency Communicate intentions clearly regarding data and models. Improve trustworthiness and product adoption. Model cards are important for documentation, transmission, and reuse. Registries are probably needed for the AI Act. 3. Interpretability Provide access to the factors that influenced the decision/prediction. More control, easier to debug. Allows explainability. Required for some products in the AI Act. 4. Explainability Explain the predictions provided by the models, work on the user interfaces. Improve adoption/trust. Human agency. 5. Vigilance Avoid possible prejudice to the users' interests, exclude discriminatory biases. Scandal prevention. AI Act compliance. Potential new customers. 6. Robustness Measure and ensure performance and stability throughout the system lifecycle. Performance. Control. 7. Sustainability Limit the system's energy consumption and carbon footprint. Financial gains, simplicity, control, acceleration. ### TYPES OF SECURITY AI FAILURE: - DATA BREACH OR LEAKAGE - NON-COMPLIANCE - RANSOMWARE / MALWARE - PHISHING - FAKE NEWS - MODEL AND DATA POISONING ### WHO'S IN CHARGE? The five foundational principles are:

· Inclusive growth, sustainable development,

and well-being: AI should advance the interests of people and the planet by fostering inclusive growth, sustainable development, and collective well-being.

. Human-centered values and fairness: Al systems must be designed to respect the rule of law, human rights, and democratic values. They should also include safeguards for fairness and justice and permit human intervention.

· Transparency and explainability: To help individuals recognize whether they are interacting with AI, AI systems should be sufficiently identifiable as such. They should also ensure transparency to allow human users to challenge negative outcomes.

· Robustness, security, and safety: Al systems must be reliable, safe, and secure throughout their life cycle, and organizations must continuously assess risks and manage the model throughout a given system's timeline.

· Accountability: Those developing, deploying, or operating AI systems should be held accountable for their actions in accordance with these principles.

Meanwhile, the five recommendations include:

· Invest in Al research and development: Encourage public and private investment in research and development for innovative and trustworthy AI.

· Foster a digital ecosystem for Al: Promote Al ecosystems that are accessible and include digital infrastructures, data, and knowledge-sharing.

· Shape an enabling policy environment for Al: Establish policy frameworks that support the deployment of trustworthy AI systems.

. Build human capacity and prepare for labor market transformation: Equip individuals with necessary AI skills and ensure a fair transition for workers.

· International co-operation for trustworthy Al: Enhance international and intersectoral cooperation to harmonize standards and approaches for trustworthy AI.

The Recommendation, in essence, sets out adaptive overarching principles to foster an environment conducive to trustworthy AI development. Recently, these principles have been updated.2145 During the OECD's May 2-3, 2024, Ministerial Council Meeting, the organization included a number of revisions to its enumerated list of principles. Among the additions were explicit references to environmental sustainability and the importance of creating interoperability among the guidelines of different jurisdictions. The revisions also included increased emphasis on safety concerns and the need to address mis- and disinformation.2146

· To establish subject fairness, we can ask if the person who is subject to a decision or action taken by or supported by an AI system perceives the process and outcome as justifiable and legitimate. To establish justifiability and legitimacy, the subject may need to know the details of how the decision or action was arrived at and what factors might have led to another outcome (e.g. a recruiting algorithm rejects a job applicant, which can be explained by showing that the applicant lacks a specifically named skill or credential). A subject also needs access to recourse if they disagree with the outcome (e.g. a job applicant has the opportunity to offer additional information or question the accuracy of the recruiting algorithm to a human with authority to alter the outcome).

· Implementer fairness can be expressed through accountability measures including processes of auditing and evaluation. Implementers are tasked with ensuring that AI systems are transparent and interpretable by those who use them and who are affected by that use. Prior to and during the use of AI, implementers should take social, economic, and political effects into account, being mindful not only of the perceived benefits of AI but also for the occurrence and risk of harm and who bears it. For example, the introduction of a criminal sentencing algorithm may produce more judicial consistency and/or streamline decision making. However, the same system may also reproduce discriminatory outcomes, such as where people of colour have received longer sentences for similar convictions as whites in white-majority countries, due to some feature of its design or the data it references. Where such conflicts occur, the functional accuracy or efficiency (if present) of an AI should be set aside and the algorithm design and data model should be thoroughly evaluated, including the decision as to whether to use it.

## CHAPTER IV TRANSPARENCY OBLIGATIONS FOR PROVIDERS AND DEPLOYERS OF CERTAIN AI SYSTEMS

## Article 50 Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems

1. Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. This obligation shall not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence.

2. Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Providers shall ensure their technical solutions are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. This obligation shall not apply to the extent the AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.

3. Deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system shall inform the natural persons exposed thereto of the operation of the system, and shall process the personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable. This obligation shall not apply to AI systems used for biometric categorisation and emotion recognition, which are permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, and in accordance with Union law.

4. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake, shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. This obligation shall not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offence. Where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the transparency obligations set out in this paragraph are limited to disclosure of the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.

Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest shall disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. This obligation shall not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences or where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and where a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.

(backpropagation) or the negative values of the reconstruction signal flowing from top to bottom (deconvolution), they mask the signal if each one of these cases occurs. The following figure depicts the guided backpropagation algorithm very well:

Figure from Springenberg et al. 2014 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6806)

Here are some of the saliency maps produced by the guided backpropagation method. As can be seen - and reported in other works too -, this algorithm is quite good at capturing high-resolution and sharp saliency maps:

Figure from Springenberg et al. 2014 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6806)

We can easily see that the saliency map is a local gradient-based backpropagation interpretation method. Although saliency maps are mostly used for interpreting CNNs, as the concept of gradient exists in all neural networks, one can use it for any arbitrary artificial neural network. Thus, it could be considered as a model-agnostic interpretation method. A similar approach is used by SHAP gradient explainer that we saw earlier.

Finally, it is worth noting that there a couple of papers that have shown saliency maps are not always reliable. Kindermans et al. 2018 (The (Un)reliability of saliency methods ) demonstrate that data preprocessing, such as subtracting the mean and normalization, can make undesirable changes in saliency maps. Ghorbani et al. 2019 (Interpretation of Neural Networks is Fragile ) also show that saliency maps are vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

D.3.c.ii. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and GRADient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM)

Class activation map (CAM) is another explanation method used for CNNs, introduced by Zhou et al. 2016 (Learning Deep Features for Discriminative Localization ). The authors of the paper have evaluated networks with the architecture similar to the Network in Network's architecture (Network In Network ). In these networks, the stack of fully connected layers at the very end of the model has been replaced by a layer named Global Average Pooling (GAP). GAP simply averages the activations of each feature map and concatenates these averages and outputs them as a vector. Then, a weighted sum of this vector is fed to the final softmax loss layer. Using this architecture, we can highlight the important regions of the image by projecting back the weights of the output on the convolutional feature maps. The following figure illustrates this process:

<!-- PageBreak -->

<!-- PageHeader: Figure from Zhou et al. 2016 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.04150) -->

An example of Class Activation Map. The figure is borrowed from Zhu et al. 2017 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.01829).

Grad-CAM is a more versatile version of CAM that can produce visual explanations for any arbitrary CNN, even if the network contains a stack of fully connected layers too (e.g. the VGG networks).

In order to get the Grad-CAM of a given image and a class of interest, we can take a quite similar approach to what we took in computing saliency maps; we let the gradients of any target concept score (logits for any class of interest such as 'human's face') flow into the final convolutional layer. We can then compute an importance score based on the gradients and produce a coarse localization map highlighting the important regions in the image for predicting that concept.

The following figure shows a visualization produced by GRAD-CAM:

GRAD-CAM visualization of an example image for the class of 'Dog'. The figure is borrowed from Selvaraju et al. 2016 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.02391)

As Grad-CAM can only produce coarse-grained visualizations, the authors have also combined guided-backpropagation with their method and propose Guided Grad- CAM. They simply do that by an element-wise multiplication of guided- backpropagation visualization and Grad-CAM's visualization:

Guided Grad-CAM as a combination of Grad-CAM and Guided Backprop. The figure is borrowed from Selvaraju et al. 2016 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.02391.pdf) with some modifications.

For more on CAM and Grad-CAM, you can read : Interpretability in Deep Learning M

So instead of using the 'predict()' result, always get the 'predict_proba()'!

However here, it must be taken into account that the majority of your users are not scientists and therefore have a biased representation of probabilities, with a tendency to overestimate low probability events and underestimate high probability events.

Thus, to simplify this notion of probability, they can be expressed not as a percentage, but in explicit terms. The reliability of the AI prediction or decision will can be "absolutely certain", "certain", "probable" or "very uncertain".

## B.1. Calibration

Some models (live SVM) can give you poor estimates of the probabilities and therefore make the interpretation of the probabilities unreliable.

We recommend calibrating your model or at least, check their reliability with calibration curves.

Lean more about calibration here:

https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~alexn/papers/calibration.icml05.crc.rev3.pdf

And on how to implement it with sklearn here:

## 1.16. Probability calibration

# C. Confidence intervals

Another interesting information to provide to the users: the confidence interval. This allows you to know on which subcategories of data the model is reliable, and for which, not so much. It is directly related to the variability in the prediction for a certain range of predictions and very much depends on how much data of each subcategories the model has been trained. For example, if a model has been trained with a lot of Caucasian faces and a few Asian ones, it will tend to be more reliable for the first class.

<!-- PageBreak -->

## C.1. Cross validation

You can get a first measure of the variability of your overall model performance by doing cross-validation (3.1. Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance ), but it is not enough as it doesn't go into the details of performance for the subcategories.

## C.2. Mapie

You can use a toolbox called Mapie (MAPIE - Model Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator - MAPIE 0.6.5 documentation ) which is a model agnostic solution that works for both regression and classification problems.

Source : Taquet et al. 2022 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

You can find a video explaining the solution here : https://crossminds.ai/video/mapie- model-agnostic-prediction-interval-estimator-614bc17e3c7a224a9090211b/

And articles here:

· With MAPIE, uncertainties are back in machine learning !

· https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

# D. Human agency/control

In a Pew Research report from 2018 on AI and the Future of Humans (Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Humans ) concern about Human agency came out as the main concern. They talk about the fear that : 'the use of Al reduces individuals' control over their lives'.

And the European Commission High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence (AI HLEG 2018 : Requirements of Trustworthy Al ) defines 'human agency and oversight' as the first of seven key elements in their "Trustworthy Al" framework. They state that 'Al systems should support human autonomy and decision-making, as prescribed by the principle of respect for human autonomy. This requires that AI systems should both act as enablers to a democratic, flourishing and equitable society by supporting the user's agency and foster fundamental rights, and allow for human oversight."

Following these reports, it is fundamental that your systems always keep the 'humans in the loop' and should never be fully autonomous. A human should always make the final decision.

<!-- PageBreak -->

This recommendation goes hand-in-hand with explicability as you should give all the necessary information to the users to make the decision.

And the design of the interface of the product or solution you are developing will be key here.

# E. Feedback loops

Because keeping people in the loop is fundamental as we have just seen, care will be taken to encourage user feedback on the solution.

## E.1. Report a mistake

If your user considers that the system has made a mistake in the prediction or decision, they must be able to express it. You should include, in the design of your solution, a way for them to do so.

This will increase the trust of your users for your solution greatly.

## E.2. Performance in production

In addition, this feedback can be used to measure the performance in production, detect drifts and give a database to eventually retrain your model.

Moreover, you can also detect bugs in the system and be able to strengthen its robustness and performance.

And here is an interesting article on the feedback loop topic: Feedback Loops-Friend or Foe?

## A. For whom?

<!-- PageBreak -->

### A.1. The regulator

As mentioned in the section about legal risks in Introduction, the new European law on AI will describe different levels of criticality for AI models. Depending on the level, complete or partial interpretability will be asked by law and in addition to documentation, some audits might occur. Therefore, interpretability will become mandatory for many AI models.

### A.2. The developer or Data Scientist

The data scientist needs to access, as best as possible, the parameters of a model to understand it, to fix possible mistakes, to improve its performance and to stay in control.

#### A.3. The main user

The user needs information in order to best use the product or solution as well as to trust its recommendation. Adoption is driven by trust and very linked to the information that will be provided. We will get into more details about that in the Explicability section of these Guidelines.

#### A.4. The final user

The final user is the person who is the subject of the prediction or decision. That can be the same person as the main user or a different one. For example, we can have a skin diagnostic solution for doctors (main users) that concerns their patients (final users). This group of people may ask for information about the decision/prediction of the algorithm and in many case, they have the legal right to know what were the factor that lead to the decision/prediction.

# B. Of what?

We can be interested to have interpretability of the whole system or just of different parts of the system. We can look to understand a single prediction, all predictions, a part of the model, the whole model, the path that the data takes along the processing pipeline ...

## B.1. Global and Local

<!-- PageBreak -->

There are two main information that we want to access when we talk about Interpretability. We want to access what factors influenced each prediction and with what extend, that is called the Local Interpretability, and we also want to know what the factors of importance for the model are, that is the Global Interpretability.

In the case of simple algorithms like the regressions, the global interpretability is directly given by the coefficients of the model after training (remember to scale or normalize your data first, overwise you will not be able to interpret the results). With sklearn, just use 'model.coef_'. You can put them in a DataFrame with the variable names for simpler visualization :

pd. DataFrame ( {"Feature" : X_train . columns . tolist () , "Coefficients" : model . coef [0]})

In the case of more complex models, we will need to use additional tools to have access to an approximation of this information, like Lime or Shap or the Feature Importance function of sklearn. N.B. LIME and SHAP are local interpretability methods but they can still be used for the global interpretability.

You can refer to the sklearn MOOC part on feature importance here for more

information: Feature importance - Scikit-learn course

For the interpretability of the predictions (local), we see the same distinction between simple and more complex algorithms. With the simple models, we can directly apply the coefficients or the rules (for simple decision tree) to the data specific for each individual prediction. For more complex algorithms, we will again use additional tools (Lime, Shap ... ).

We will come back to the tools in more details in a dedicated section.

# C. Why not interpretable?

## C.1. The data complexity

There are different ways in which the data itself can make the system hard to interpret.

Some variables may contain information that is difficult to comprehend, for example medical or scientific information or expert technical measurements.

Moreover, during the Feature Engineering of the model construction, we may apply manipulations to the data that may lead to a loss of meaning. For example taking the log of a measure, using a dimension reduction method (i.e. PCA), combining variables ...

<!-- PageBreak -->

Finally, the storage of the data can add to the complexity if we lose the lineage and the contextual information that goes with it.

trustworthiness and safety of generative Al models.294 It makes it very difficult for third parties to assess a model's performance and its potential to cause harm-assessments that require knowing the key features of a model. This is particularly problematic as downstream applications are based on foundation models. If the original developers of a foundation model do not completely disclose these structural elements, downstream developers and users are even less likely to understand them, particularly if information about the model's characteristics is lacking.295 This may result in some risks being difficult or impossible to prepare for or mitigate.

In this context, researchers and experts have advocated for legal safe harbors296 or government-mediated access regimes297 to enable independent assessment efforts. These proposals aim to allow independent researchers and auditors to analyze models with full access in a secured environment, without making the code and weights public. Simultaneously, many Al experts argue for the benefits of open models, which enhance transparency and interpretability (see section 2.3.2.).

The call for greater transparency is also echoed by employees of leading Al companies. On June 4, 2024, several former employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind published an open letter titled "A Right to Warn about Advanced Artificial Intelligence."298 They highlighted the significant risks posed by advanced Al technology, such as exacerbating existing inequalities, enabling manipulation and misinformation, and losing control over autonomous Al systems, potentially

leading to human extinction. The authors emphasized that these dangers could be mitigated with adequate guidance from the scientific community, policymakers, and the public. However, they pointed out that, despite possessing substantial nonpublic information about their systems' capabilities, limitations, and associated risks, Al companies have only weak obligations to share this information and strong financial incentives to resist effective oversight. As a result, the signatories advocate for robust whistleblower protections for employees and urge Al companies to cultivate a "culture of open criticism" that encourages, rather than penalizes, those who voice their concerns. They specifically call for the establishment of a verifiably anonymous process for employees to raise risk-related issues with the company's board, regulators, and independent organizations with relevant expertise.

Currently, it seems that the industry, or parts of it, is making efforts to enhance transparency. Results of a study released by Stanford University's Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM) in October 2023 found that 10 leading developers of the most powerful Al models satisfied an average of only 37 out of 100 indicators of model transparency.299 Amazon performed the worst, meeting just 12% of the indicators, while Meta performed the best at 54%, followed closely by Hugging Face at 53%. OpenAl met 47% of the indicators. However, by May 2024, the index showed significant improvement, with an average score of 58 out of 100. Hugging Face now leads with 85%, Meta is at 60%, and Amazon, although still the worst performer, improved to 41%.300

#### 3.1.3.A. The black box problem

Opacity surrounding the technical, internal decision- making processes of generative Al models is popularly known as the "black box problem."277 Generative Al models, most ubiquitously built on deep neural networks with hundreds of billions of internal connections,278 have become so complex that their internal decision-making processes are no longer traceable or interpretable to even the most advanced expert observers. This means that, while the inputs and outputs of a system can be observed, developers cannot explain in detail why specific inputs correspond to specific outputs.279

Increasing interpretability (i.e., the comprehension of how an Al model generates a specific output) is crucial. For developers and model trainers, understanding how models make decisions allows them to identify and correct biases, errors, and unintended behaviors, leading to more robust and efficient systems. This ability to anticipate and mitigate errors ensures that Al outputs are accurate and ethically sound. For lay people who use Al models, interpretability empowers them to make informed decisions and detect when the Al might be malfunctioning or producing biased outputs, enabling timely corrective actions. This reduces the risk of relying on faulty Al recommendations and fosters confidence in using these technologies. For individuals impacted by Al decisions, such as in healthcare, education, and finance, interpretability ensures that they can understand and challenge incorrect outcomes. Overall, increasing

interpretability helps prevent and mitigate unforeseen negative consequences, making Al systems more transparent, reliable, and aligned with societal values.

In the future, Al models may become less opaque. The field of explainable AI (XAI) seeks to develop new techniques and methods to improve the ability of users to comprehend the inner workings of Al models. 280 For instance, Anthropic has achieved a breakthrough to enhance the interpretability of language models.281 Instead of focusing on individual neurons, researchers at Anthropic analyze groups of neurons as features, revealing clearer patterns. Recently, Anthropic's researchers managed to extract millions of features from one of their Al models, creating a rough conceptual map of the model's internal states. 282 This approach may improve transparency and control over Al behavior.

#### 3.1.3.B. Industry opacity

Opacity is not solely due to the technological complexity that limits developers' and users' understanding of how generative models function on a technical level. It is further exacerbated by the practices of organizations and companies that are advancing the field. Many are private companies that choose to withhold from the public many of the precise characteristics of their most advanced models. Al developers cite both near-term competition and security risks to justify withholding many vital details of their models from the general public. Though not often acknowledged, legal issues are also a likely influence for

results.content: ## · And mitigating AI risks is a true challenge in business adoption Hallucination, bias, confidentiality: these are the risks and limits that are holding companies back from using AI, through a healthy respect for both the regulatory framework, and a context where the acceptable margin of error in decision-making is low. So what do we mean by this? · Hallucination: generative Als are based on a multitude of documents. When the next word to predict matches the truth, all is well. But otherwise? They must choose one option, and can hallucinate untruths with great aplomb. Users therefore need to be trained to use these AIs properly, and to verify every single claim they make. . Bias: they are rarely intentional, but algorithmic biases are based on data reflecting human practice. The system can therefore discriminate against a specific group of people. A major obstacle for businesses is to identify potential biases (lack of qualified data), raise awareness among employees and have the resources to do so (a dedicated inclusive team, for instance, or a taxonomy programmed with contextual information), and then deal with the biases. . Privacy: The confidentiality rules of GenAl, and ChatGPT in particular, are still poorly understood. Bear in mind that any data and/or code sent to one of these platforms is likely to be used for subsequent training, which raises issues of confidentiality of corporate data (or that of its customers) and intellectual property. Overcoming these risks is not an option, it's a sine qua non condition for some businesses. However, the adoption of AI itself is facilitated when it is designed responsibly from the outset: ethical standards reinforce confidence in its use; responsible practices in critical sectors such as human resources guarantee a positive and equitable societal impact; operational excellence prevents abuse and ensures that the AI is beneficial and reliable... Adopting a responsible AI is thus becoming a crucial approach to minimizing risk. ## . Key Issue ### How do we turn this AI revolution into a competitive advantage? We need new "software" to tackle this profound change in the way we work, and even in the way we do business. New responsible governance must overcome all the risks generated by the use of AI and generative AI. By evolving into an "AI-ready" business, organizations put in place the conditions that will enable them to meet the key business challenges of the future, and perpetuate their business practices and even their business model. It's a moment of truth for organizations: yes, there is a turning point ahead; yet it does not have to be a problem: by implementing a "responsible-by-design" approach, organizations are better equipped to deal with the risks -not just compliance risks, but also business risks- created by the exploding use of Al (see pillars). Ekimetrics intends to accompany this revolution with a simple, easy-to-understand framework to support these organizations in their AI transformation and the use of these technologies. We have therefore developed 7 pillars of responsible AI, designed to create this competitive edge (see next chapter). ## · Empower business with AI and GenAI solutions through responsible governance Anticipate future regulations, limit the risk of damage to image and reputation, improve the efficiency, accuracy and durability of models, all while generating value: to meet all these challenges, Ekimetrics has developed 7 pillars of responsible governance, which can be considered true operational and business tools. THE 7 PILLARS OF RESPONSIBLE AI AND THEIR BUSINESS ADVANTAGES 1. Security Ensure the security of personal and sensitive data. GDPR compliance. Data Clean Rooms: value of personal data. 2. Transparency Communicate intentions clearly regarding data and models. Improve trustworthiness and product adoption. Model cards are important for documentation, transmission, and reuse. Registries are probably needed for the AI Act. 3. Interpretability Provide access to the factors that influenced the decision/prediction. More control, easier to debug. Allows explainability. Required for some products in the AI Act. 4. Explainability Explain the predictions provided by the models, work on the user interfaces. Improve adoption/trust. Human agency. 5. Vigilance Avoid possible prejudice to the users' interests, exclude discriminatory biases. Scandal prevention. AI Act compliance. Potential new customers. 6. Robustness Measure and ensure performance and stability throughout the system lifecycle. Performance. Control. 7. Sustainability Limit the system's energy consumption and carbon footprint. Financial gains, simplicity, control, acceleration. ### TYPES OF SECURITY AI FAILURE: - DATA BREACH OR LEAKAGE - NON-COMPLIANCE - RANSOMWARE / MALWARE - PHISHING - FAKE NEWS - MODEL AND DATA POISONING ### WHO'S IN CHARGE? Retraining can be costly from a purely computational perspective, but it is more common to be expensive from a human labor perspective.

An MLOps system will enable setting up a pipeline that retrains, evaluates, and deploys a model without human intervention, and it can be triggered automatically to do.

In more computationally heavy cases, like deep learning, the cost considerations will be more relevant. Sophisticated monitoring systems will allow teams to trigger retraining more deliberately, and for certain types of models, this will be a must to avoid unnecessary costs.

# C. Adversarial environments

Certain system works in adversarial environments where the relationship between the subject and the model is somehow antagonistic. Examples of such domains could be fraud detection, spam detection, comment moderation, and search engine ranking algorithms.

Most adversarial attacks usually aim to deteriorate the performance of classifiers on specific tasks, essentially to "fool" the machine learning algorithm.

Some of the most common threat models in adversarial machine learning include evasion attacks, data poisoning attacks and model extraction.

## C.1. Evasion Attacks

Evasion attacks are the most prevalent and most researched types of attacks. The attacker manipulates the data during deployment to deceive previously trained classifiers. Since they are performed during the deployment phase, they are the most practical types of attacks and the most used attacks on intrusion and malware scenarios. The attackers often attempt to evade detection by obfuscating the content of malware or spam emails. Therefore, samples are modified to evade detection as they are classified as legitimate without directly impacting the training data. Examples of evasion are spoofing attacks against biometric verification systems.

## C.2. Poisoning Attacks

<!-- PageBreak -->

The attacker influences the training data or its labels to cause the model to underperform during deployment. Hence, Poisoning is essentially adversarial contamination of training data. As ML systems can be re-trained using data collected during operation, an attacker may poison the data by injecting malicious samples during operation, which subsequently disrupt or influence re-training.

## C.3. Model Extraction

Model stealing or model extraction involves an attacker probing a black box machine learning system in order to either reconstruct the model or extract the data it was trained on. This is especially significant when either the training data or the model itself is sensitive and confidential. Model extraction attacks can be used, for instance, to steal a stock market prediction model, which the adversary could use for their own financial benefit.

## C.4. Defenses Against Adversarial Examples with Adversarial Training

Nowadays, adversarial training is the most effective defense strategy. Adversarial examples are generated and used when training the model. Intuitively, if the model sees adversarial examples during training, its performance at prediction time will be better for adversarial examples generated in the same way.

Ideally, we would like to employ any known attack method to generate adversarial examples during training.

The Wikipedia page on Adversarial attacks is very well done, you can read it for much more information on this interesting field: Adversarial machine learning

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.

To address the technical aspects of how to measure the appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness set out in paragraph 1 and any other relevant performance metrics, the Commission shall, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, encourage, as appropriate, the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies.

5. High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.

The technical solutions aiming to ensure the cybersecurity of high-risk AI systems shall be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks.

The technical solutions to address AI specific vulnerabilities shall include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning), or pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws.

# 6- Robustness

Robustness is about measuring and ensuring the performance of the system and its stability all along its life cycle. It mostly concerns observing its behavior through probes and monitoring and adjusting by retraining if necessary. We will also briefly talk about possible adversarial attacks.

# A. Observability

AI observability is the collection of statistics, performance data, and metrics from every part of an ML system. This allows to deliver actionable insights to improve the performance of the system and fix bugs or problems.

Although ML monitoring and observability seem similar, observability denotes a bigger picture with testing, validation, and preparedness for unpredictable failure modes.

But it all starts by measuring and monitoring.

## A.1. Data Monitoring

Data skew occurs when the Machine Learning model is trained on the data that does not represent the live data.

There are various reasons why this can happen:

· Training data is designed incorrectly: Distributions of the training data variables are different from the real data variables' distribution.

· Non-availability of feature in production: Sometimes, at the production level, the model has to predict data on which it is not trained. This means that we have to remove the feature, change it with some other variable in production, or re-create that feature by combining other production features.

· Data Dependencies: Machine learning models usually use variables that are created or stored by other systems. Suppose there are any changes in the system on which data is generated or the code implementation of a feature changes. In that case, it will produce slightly different results, or might the definition of a feature change

· Upstream data changes: Changes in upstream data refer to operational data changes in the data pipeline. It is very common in practice that the data science team usually doesn't control every system from where input data comes. For instance, a completely siloed data engineering team changes a variable from Fahrenheit to Celcius even though the rest of the data is still stored in Fahrenheit. This slight change in one variable might impact an overall if one tried to find the average temperature.

<!-- PageBreak -->

· Data Integrity: Data inconsistencies can often go unnoticed in deployed Al systems. Data science teams need to detect feature errors like missing values, type mismatch, and range anomalies to reduce overall issue resolution time.
